The Thirteenth through Twenty-third Chapters Contain Prophecies as to Foreign Nations.--The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Twenty-seventh Chapters as to Babylon and Assyria.</title> <div sID="gen13951" type="x-p"/> The predictions as to foreign nations are for the sake of the covenant people, to preserve them from despair, or reliance on human confederacies, and to strengthen their faith in God: also in order to extirpate narrow-minded nationality: God is Jehovah to Israel, not for Israel's sake alone, but that He may be thereby Elohim to the nations. These prophecies are in their right chronological place, in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign; then the nations of Western Asia, on the Tigris and Euphrates, first assumed a most menacing aspect.<div eID="gen13951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13952" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8548"/><hi type="bold">1. burden--</hi>weighty or mournful prophecy [Grotius]. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 13 Is 13:1-22 . The Thirteenth through Twenty-third Chapters Contain Prophecies as to Foreign Nations.--The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Twenty-seventh Chapters as to Babylon and Assyria. The predictions as to foreign nations are for the sake of the covenant people, to preserve them from despair, or reliance on human confederacies, and to strengthen their faith in God: also in order to extirpate narrow-minded nationality: God is Jehovah to Israel, not for Israel's sake alone, but that He may be thereby Elohim to the nations. These prophecies are in their right chronological place, in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign; then the nations of Western Asia, on the Tigris and Euphrates, first assumed a most menacing aspect. 1. burden-- weighty or mournful prophecy [Grotius]. Otherwise, simply, the prophetical declaration, from a Hebrew root to put forth with the voice anything, as in Nu 23:7 [Maurer]. of Babylon-- concerning Babylon.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8549"/><div sID="gen13954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8549"/><hi type="bold">2. Lift ... banner--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">11:10</reference>).<div eID="gen13954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the high mountain--</hi>rather, "a bare (literally, "bald," that is, without trees) mountain"; from it the banner could be seen afar off, so as to rally together the peoples against Babylon.<div eID="gen13955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto them--</hi>unto the Medes (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Is 13:17</reference>), the assailants of Babylon. It is remarkable that Isaiah does not foretell here the Jews' captivity in Babylon, but presupposes that event, and throws himself beyond, predicting another event still more future, the overthrow of the city of Israel's oppressors. It was now one hundred seventy-four years before the event.<div eID="gen13956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake ... hand--</hi>beckon with the hand--wave the hand to direct the nations to march against Babylon.<div eID="gen13957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nobles--</hi>Babylonian. Rather, in a bad sense, tyrants; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.5">Is 14:5</reference>, "rulers" in parallelism to "the wicked"; and <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference> [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13958" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 2. Lift ... banner-- ( Is 5:26 ; 11:10 ). the high mountain-- rather, "a bare (literally, "bald," that is, without trees) mountain"; from it the banner could be seen afar off, so as to rally together the peoples against Babylon. unto them-- unto the Medes ( Is 13:17 ), the assailants of Babylon. It is remarkable that Isaiah does not foretell here the Jews' captivity in Babylon, but presupposes that event, and throws himself beyond, predicting another event still more future, the overthrow of the city of Israel's oppressors. It was now one hundred seventy-four years before the event. shake ... hand-- beckon with the hand--wave the hand to direct the nations to march against Babylon. nobles-- Babylonian. Rather, in a bad sense, tyrants; as in Is 14:5 , "rulers" in parallelism to "the wicked"; and Job 21:28 [Maurer].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8550"/><div sID="gen13959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8550"/><hi type="bold">3. sanctified ones--</hi>the Median and Persian soldiers solemnly set apart by Me for the destruction of Babylon, not inwardly "sanctified," but designated to fulfil God's holy purpose (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jr 51:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.9">Joe 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.11">11</reference>; where the Hebrew for prepare war is "sanctify" war).<div eID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for mine anger--</hi>to execute it.<div eID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice in my highness--</hi>"Those who are made to triumph for My honor" [Horsley]. The heathen Medes could not be said to "rejoice in God's highness" Maurer translates, "My haughtily exulting ones" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.11">Zep 3:11</reference>); a special characteristic of the Persians [Herodotus,1.88]. They rejoiced in their own highness, but it was His that they were unconsciously glorifying. <div eID="gen13961" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8556"/><div sID="gen13977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8556"/><hi type="bold">9. cruel--</hi>not strictly, but unsparingly just; opposed to mercy. Also answering to the cruelty (in the strict sense) of Babylon towards others (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Is 14:17</reference>) now about to be visited on itself.<div eID="gen13977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the land--</hi>"the earth" [Horsley]. The language of <reference osisRef="Isa.13.9-Isa.13.13">Is 13:9-13</reference> can only primarily and partially apply to Babylon; fully and exhaustively, the judgments to come, hereafter, on the whole earth. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Is 13:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mt 24:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.12">Re 8:12</reference>. The sins of Babylon, arrogancy (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Is 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Is 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7">47:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">8</reference>), cruelty, false worship (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jr 50:38</reference>), persecution of the people of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Is 47:6</reference>), are peculiarly characteristic of the Antichristian world of the latter days (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.32-Dan.11.37">Da 11:32-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">18:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9-Rev.7.14">7, 9-14</reference>, 24). <div eID="gen13978" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. cruel-- not strictly, but unsparingly just; opposed to mercy. Also answering to the cruelty (in the strict sense) of Babylon towards others ( Is 14:17 ) now about to be visited on itself. the land-- "the earth" [Horsley]. The language of Is 13:9-13 can only primarily and partially apply to Babylon; fully and exhaustively, the judgments to come, hereafter, on the whole earth. Compare Is 13:10 with Mt 24:29 ; Re 8:12 . The sins of Babylon, arrogancy ( Is 13:11 ; Is 14:11 ; 47:7 , 8 ), cruelty, false worship ( Jr 50:38 ), persecution of the people of God ( Is 47:6 ), are peculiarly characteristic of the Antichristian world of the latter days ( Da 11:32-37 ; Re 17:3 , 6 ; 18:6 , 7, 9-14 , 24).

entries.content_plain: 22. wild beasts of the islands-- rather, "jackals"; called by the Arabs "sons of howling"; an animal midway between a fox and a wolf [Bochart and Maurer]. cry-- rather, "answer," "respond" to each other, as wolves do at night, producing a most dismal effect. dragons-- serpents of various species, which hiss and utter dolorous sounds. Fable gave them wings, because they stand with much of the body elevated and then dart swiftly. navigation_sections.title: CHAPTER 13
navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 13 Is 13:1-22 . The Thirteenth through Twenty-third Chapters Contain Prophecies as to Foreign Nations.--The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Twenty-seventh Chapters as to Babylon and Assyria. The predictions as to foreign nations are for the sake of the covenant people, to preserve them from despair, or reliance on human confederacies, and to strengthen their faith in God: also in order to extirpate narrow-minded nationality: God is Jehovah to Israel, not for Israel's sake alone, but that He may be thereby Elohim to the nations. These prophecies are in their right chronological place, in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign; then the nations of Western Asia, on the Tigris and Euphrates, first assumed a most menacing aspect.
